record.paper_title: Nuclei of Seyfert galaxies and QSOs - Central engine & conditions of star formation: Workshop summary and open questions
record.context_brief: nuclear star clusters and massive black holes
record.original_question: Do very massive black holes inhibit the formation of nuclear star clusters, or are nuclear star clusters instead disrupted during the growth of the central black hole?

evidence.quote: The question about formation of Nuclear Star Clusters (NSC) is also intriguing (Capuzzo’s talk) [...] There are galaxies with NSC and with no BHs present (but they might be just below our current detection limit), and there are some galaxies where BH and NSC are present simultaneously.
So, do very massive black holes somehow prevent formation of an NSC or are they disrupted during the process of black hole growth?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A nuclear star cluster (NSC) is a dense, compact stellar cluster located at the photometric and dynamical center of a galaxy, with typical effective radii of a few parsecs and stellar masses in the range 10^6–10^8 solar masses. A central massive black hole (MBH) is a black hole with mass typically exceeding 10^6 solar masses residing at a galactic nucleus. Observations indicate that some galaxies host an NSC without any detected MBH, some host an MBH without an NSC, and some host both simultaneously. In particular, galaxies hosting very massive central black holes (with masses exceeding roughly 10^8–10^9 solar masses) tend to lack detectable nuclear star clusters.

Determine which of the following two scenarios accounts for the observed absence of nuclear star clusters in galaxies hosting very massive central black holes:

(a) The presence of a very massive central black hole prevents the formation of a nuclear star cluster in the first place (for example, by suppressing or disrupting the inflow of gas and the dynamical conditions necessary for NSC assembly via gas-rich in situ formation or via the inspiral of globular clusters);

(b) Nuclear star clusters do form in such galaxies but are subsequently destroyed or dissolved during the growth of the central black hole (for example, through tidal disruption of cluster stars, heating by the deepening potential, or scattering processes associated with black hole mergers and accretion).

Provide a physical mechanism, supported by dynamical and observational arguments, that distinguishes between scenarios (a) and (b), and identify which of the two (or what combination) is responsible.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature (e.g., a 2024 MNRAS simulation study of low-mass galaxies, a 2020 A&A Review on nuclear star clusters, and 2021 work on NSC star formation histories) continues to discuss both possibilities — that interactions with very massive black holes may destroy NSCs or inhibit their growth in the most massive galaxies — but no single mechanism has been definitively established. The question of whether very massive MBHs prevent NSC formation or disrupt pre-existing NSCs remains an active research topic without a settled answer.

status_evidence.title: Nuclear star clusters (Neumayer, Seth, Böker review)
status_evidence.snippet: Interactions with supermassive black holes were thought to destroy NSCs or inhibit NSC growth in the most massive galaxies, possibly explaining the negligible nucleation fraction for galaxies with stellar masses greater than 10^11 solar masses.
status_evidence.claim: Both inhibition and destruction scenarios are still discussed; the explanation for absence of NSCs in very massive galaxies remains uncertain.

status_evidence.title: The importance of nuclear star clusters for massive black hole growth and nuclear star formation in simulated low-mass galaxies
status_evidence.snippet: NSCs boost nuclear star formation and MBH accretion; without NSCs, low-mass MBHs do not grow.
status_evidence.claim: Active modeling of the NSC–MBH coevolution problem indicates the question is still open.
